title: Intermediate/Advanced Ballet with Dean Vollick
description: Class begins with a thorough set of exercises at the barre that last from 30 to 45 minutes. Centre practice follows, and may consist of a battement tendu exercise, a battement jeté exercise, a grand battement exercise, small and/or large adage, stationary turns, traveling turns, and petite and grand allegro enchaînement (small and big jumps). Classes are structured so that the dancer warms up their feet, legs, hips and upper body gradually. As class progresses there are more changes of weight and eventually, sudden changes of direction. Live music is provided by a pianist, that ranges from classical pieces to selections from ballet repertoire to improvisational contemporary music. Cost: $20 Single Class | $15.00 barre | 5-class package $90.00 *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. Please register in studio with the class assistant Accepted Payments: Cash, Check, Venmo What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Ballet originated in the Italian Renaissance courts around 1500 as large balls or spectacles that were performed by members of the royal court. The French king, Louis XIV, created the first academy and the positions, steps, and movements of the ballet were collected and codified. The spectacles began to be performed by artists that were trained in the academy, originally as part of an opera, and later as ballets that told a story through music, mime, and dance. Over the centuries ballet has influenced folk dance styles of many (mainly European) nations and, more recently, has been influenced by folk, modern, and contemporary forms of dance from all countries. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I had a professional dance career that spanned more than twenty years and included company work in both ballet and contemporary companies as well as dancing, choreographing, and teaching as a freelance artist.

title: Multi-Site Exhibition Tour: Alfonso Ossorio: Line and Lineage and Knowledge Is Myth: Chimeric Continuities
description: Join Ally Cirelli, curator of Alfonso Ossorio: Line and Lineage (October 23, 2026–April 11, 2027) at the Harvard Art Museums, and Danni Shen, curator of Knowledge Is Myth: Chimeric Continuities (October 1–December 13, 2026) at the Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts, for a multi-site tour of the two interconnected exhibitions. At the Harvard Art Museums exhibition, we will explore the experimental processes of modern artist Alfonso Ossorio and work by contemporary artists Enzo Camacho and Ami Lien that respond to his artistic legacy in the Philippines. Continuing to the Carpenter Center, we will view more works by Ossorio, Camacho, and Lien as well as other contemporary artists working with mythology. Throughout the tour, Cirelli and Shen will highlight the intergenerational connections made by these artists through material experimentation. Led by: Ally Cirelli, Cunningham Senior Curatorial Assistant for the Collection, Division of Modern and Contemporary Art, Harvard Art Museums Danni Shen, Senior Curatorial and Public Programs Assistant, Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts Alfonso Ossorio: Line and Lineage is made possible through the generous support of the Ossorio Fund, with additional support from the Recharge Foundation Fund for Contemporary Art. , Fund for Modern and Contemporary Art.

title: The 2026 Picower Lecture with Richard L. Huganir, PhD, Johns Hopkins University
description: The 2026 Picower Lecture with Richard L. Huganir, PhD, Johns Hopkins University Speaker: Richard L. Huganir, Ph.D., Bloomberg Distinguished Professor, Department of Neuroscience and Psychological and Brain Sciences; Director, Department of Neuroscience; Kavli Neuroscience Discovery Institute, Johns Hopkins UniversityDate: Wednesday, October 28, 2026Time: 4:00pmLocation: Singleton Auditorium (46-3002, Third Fl of MIT Building 46)Faculty Host: Linlin FanPlease Note: This seminar is offered in person only. Neurotransmitter Receptors: Synaptopathies and Synaptic Engrams Abstract: Neurotransmitter receptors mediate signal transduction at synaptic connections between neurons in the brain. My laboratory has been elucidating the molecular mechanisms that regulate glutamate receptors, the major excitatory neurotransmitter receptors in the central nervous system. We are particularly interested in how glutamate receptor regulation is involved in learning and memory, and other higher brain processes. We have recently focused on AMPA-type glutamate receptors and studied their regulation by posttranslational modifications and by various AMPA receptor-interacting proteins. Regulation of AMPA receptors by these mechanisms modulates their proper subcellular trafficking and synaptic targeting and is critical for several forms of synaptic plasticity, learning, and memory. Recent evidence has indicated that AMPA receptor plasticity may be disrupted in several neurological and psychiatric disorders. Specifically, mutations in the AMPA receptor and its interacting proteins, such as the synaptic RasGAP SynGAP1, are associated with cognitive disorders, including intellectual disability, autism, and schizophrenia. Based on these findings, we have recently been developing potential therapies for these devastating disorders. title: Richard P. Stanley Seminar in Combinatorics
description: Speaker: Ariana Chin (UCLA) Title: Zamolodchikov Periodic Cluster Algebras Abstract: In 2007, Fomin and Zelevinsky introduced the bipartite belt, a sequence of bipartite cluster mutations whose exchange relations form a discrete dynamical system. When the system is periodic, we call thisZamolodchikov periodicity. In this talk, we discuss the classification of all Zamolodchikov periodic cluster algebras, with connections to W-graphs, root systems, and maximal green sequences. We observe that there is a natural red-blue statistic on the associated tropical dynamics that is homomesic, and use laminations to prove it for finite type. This gives a natural bijection between colored mutations in the dynamical system and roots in the associated root system.

title: MIT Music Tech Speaker Series: Andrew McPherson
description: Enacted, not Extracted: Designing and Performing with Music-Analytical Concepts This is a talk about designing musical instruments and the delicate interplay of artistic and technical ways of thinking. All instruments, and especially digital ones, entail a balance between design and analysis, with instruments relying on symbolic or numerical models of music in order to create it, as exemplified in the venerable MIDI standard. However, no system is ever devoid of sociocultural context, and even the simplest technologies when examined in situ can exhibit fascinating complexity. This talk will begin with a stubbornly contrarian take on some seemingly obvious premises of musical ontology. Physicist and feminist theorist Karen Barad writes that, "language has been granted too much power." I would like to propose that as designers and researchers, we can let words about music take precedence over the messy and open-ended experience of making music, and that becoming overly preoccupied with language risks propagating clichés and reinforcing cultural stereotypes. Drawing on recent scholarship in human-computer interaction, and science and technology studies, I will recount some alternative approaches and possible futures for designing music technology when technical and cultural factors are inextricably entangled. I will illustrate these ideas with recent projects from the Augmented Instruments Laboratory, with a focus on rich bidirectional couplings between digital and analog electronics, acoustics, and human creative experience. Speaker Bio: Andrew McPherson (https://andrewmcpherson.org) is Professor of Design Engineering and Music at Imperial College London, where he leads the Augmented Instruments Laboratory (https://instrumentslab.org), a research team creating new musical instruments, studying the encounters between musicians and instruments, and developing high-performance technologies for real-time interactive audio. title: The Ambivalences of Return: Diasporic Utopias and Anti-Migrant Policies
description: "Return" is a central notion for thinking about the diasporic condition in general (W. Safran). In the "radical imaginations" (R.D.G. Kelley) of the Black Americas of the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries, from Black nationalism to Pan-Africanism, as well as in African anticolonialisms, "return" refers to a shared political dream: making Africa a land of hospitality for all Africans and/or Black people dispersed across the world. Return carries an ideal of reparative justice: reuniting, on the land from which they were torn, those whom slavery and colonization had separated. Within these traditions, however, the idea is fraught with tensions, and for those who experience return to the continent, it often appears as a myth (S. Hartman, M. Condé). In the aftermath of the Second World War, the idea of "return" was elevated to the status of a right. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 recognizes everyone's right to return to their country, and that same year, in the context of the war in Palestine, United Nations General Assembly Resolution 194 affirmed it for Palestinian refugees. From then on, the term became the object of competing claims to the same land, as illustrated two years later by the Israeli Law of Return. This term, born of the experience of violence and carrying a constantly renewed desire for justice within diasporized communities separated from a homeland, whether real or imagined, takes on a radically antithetical meaning in twenty-first-century migration policies, particularly in Europe. In 2026, in the European Union's "Return Regulation," which complements the Pact on Migration and Asylum, "return" appears as a euphemism for "removal" or "deportation," to a land that is not necessarily the land of origin. Warmup Footwork Review Foundational move for Level 1 On2 Linear Salsa (of which there are 7) Dance with Music Philosophically things to be on the lookout for, the importance of melding footwork and partner-work when dancing Salsa, the importance of spaced repetition, the importance of tying everything to Social dancing, and personal convolutional schemes to try to attenuate the lead/follow dichotomy. No partner required. *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. *Students who purchase a membership for the Dance Complex will get that $25 taken off their 10 class new student rate, bringing it down to $85. Cost: $23 Single Class | $85 for 5-Class Package | $130 for 10-Class Package | $110 for new student 10-class package Cash, Venmo (@Brendan-Folan), Zelle (bjfoley21@gmail.com) REGISTRATION: Not Required, Drop-Ins Welcome What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Linear Salsa is a hybrid dance that comes from Mambo (a Cuban style that was popularized in the 1950’s NYC Palladium). NY Mambo is a marriage of footwork and partner-work from Cuba (Aftro-Cuban movements, Cuban Son) and the U.S. (Jazz, Swing). Salsa is a marketing term popularized in the 1970’s to commodify all Latin music and dance to a U.S. audience. Circular Salsa primarily comes from the Cuban dance Casino, which itself originates from Cuban Son. Salsa is by nature transformational, multinational, and multigenerational, embodying the shared heritage of Latin music. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I was the assistant teacher of this class for over 2 years under Ricardo Contreras. I’ve been taking classes from Juan Lopez for over 7 years. I started my Salsa journey learning New York Style Salsa On2 in Worcester. I also work at the Havana Club

title: Live Blues & Roots Music Returns to Harvard Square: Wednesday Nights @ The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar
description: The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar and The Barrett Anderson Band are excited to announce a new weekly series, Blues & Roots Wednesdays , bringing live music back home to historic Harvard Square. “Cambridge, our fair city, and I share deep roots, and I’m thrilled to find a new musical home at The Sea Hag,” says Massachusetts-based singer/guitarist, Barrett Anderson. “Good music and good food are two of our most basic, fundamental needs,” he continues, “What great joy they give us. I am so happy to revel in that every Wednesday night with my dearest musical friends, and Kari and her incredible team at The Sea Hag. We go way back together, and I can’t imagine all the fun we have ahead.” Indeed, Anderson has strong connections to this scene. He remembers: “My first professional experience came when I was 15, backing up Muddy Waters’ band alums Pinetop Perkins and Bob Margolin at the original House of Blues on Winthrop Street. A few months after that I began busking, you’d often find me in Brattle Square or by the pit. This would have been mid/late 90s.” While still a teen, Anderson was a member of The Monster Mike Welch Band and Ronnie Earl & The Broadcasters (“Ronnie was my guitar hero. Then he was my teacher, then my boss. Now he’s my musical Father,” Anderson says), before eventually starting The Barrett Anderson Band in 2007. Anderson won a Boston Music Award (2013 Blues Artist of the Year), was on the Billboard charts (2020’s live album Hynoboogie spent 3 weeks on the Billboard Blues Album chart, peaking at #6), and was nominated for a Blues Music Award (2023 Band of the Year with Anthony Geraci & The Boston Blues All-Stars), all the while playing nationally, internationally, and locally in Cambridge and the greater Boston area. In addition to the musical roots, long-time locals may recognize Anderson from a decade serving tables and bartending at The Sea Hag’s sister establishment, Grendel’s Den, or from Abodeon, the mid-century modern shop started by his family. title: Wendy S. Walters at Harvard Book Store
description: Harvard Book Store welcomes Wendy S. Walters —associate professor of nonfiction in the Writing Program of the School of the Arts at Columbia University and author of Multiply/Divide: On the American Real and Surreal —for a discussion of her new book, A Dead White: An Argument Against White Paint. About A Dead White An impassioned, boundary-pushing work of criticism traversing an array of subjects, from fine arts to design to architecture, taking aim at the ubiquity of white paint in our society and what its prevalence reveals about our values. It’s hard to identify a material that takes up more sensory space and has received less critical examination than white paint. As the default color of our built environment, it asks us to believe that it’s neutral—that it has no signifiers or, perhaps more troublingly, that what it does signify, whether it be calmness, cleanliness, blankness, or purity, is unassailable and value-free. In this expansive, impassioned examination, cultural critic Wendy S. Walters interrogates all that we have taken for granted about the substance that colors, or fails to color, the structures and objects that surround us—and what the collective impulse toward white paint can tell us about culture, politics, and individual desire. Tracing the unquantifiable impact of white paint on our lived environment and in our collective imaginary, A Dead White braids together multiple narrative threads and associations. Exploring the role of white paint in art history, architecture, and consumer culture, it follows its influence into the home, the halls of the workplace, the galleries and studios of the contemporary art world, and larger forums of mass culture and national identity, never losing sight of how this cultural inclination manifests in our choices and habits as individuals. title: Hunter Flynn: Back to My Roots Tour
description: Hunter Flynn: Back to My Roots Tour With special guest Evan Cyote Presented by The Rockwell and Peachtree Entertainment. Hunter Flynn is a Kentucky-born singer-songwriter and visual artist whose work resonates with emotional honesty and a deep connection to Appalachian culture. Raised in Pulaski County, Flynn’s path to music and art wasn’t a straight line—it was forged through adversity and personal transformation. In early 2022, after surviving a life-altering car accident, he decided to fully embrace his creative passions, launching a music career rooted in authenticity, vulnerability, and soul. Drawing inspiration from the landscapes and stories of Appalachia, Flynn blends elements of folk, country, soul, and gospel into a genre-defying sound he calls Appalachian Soul Music. His lyrics, often reflective and raw, tell stories of pain, redemption, resilience, and identity—underscored by his powerful vocals and minimalist arrangements. These qualities are showcased in his debut EP, Appalachian Soul, released in May 2023, which quickly gained traction for its emotional depth and stripped-back sincerity. Learn more about Hunter Flynn and his music at www.hunterflynn.com . description: Explore photographs through the lens of teen tragedy songs (known as “death discs”), hauntology, and postwar American nostalgia. title: Evening With a Laureate: Simon Johnson
description: Thursday, October 29, 2026 | 5PM - 9PM AI & The Global Economy - What's Next? Join us for an extraordinary evening with 2024 Nobel Laureate Simon Johnson, the Ronald A. Kurtz Professor of Entrepreneurship at the MIT Sloan School of Management. Professor Johnson first came to MIT as a doctoral student, earning his PhD in Economics before joining the Institute's faculty, where he has spent decades advancing research on economic growth, technology, public policy, and the transformative impact of artificial intelligence. In 2024, he was awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, alongside fellow economists Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson, for their groundbreaking research on how institutions shape prosperity. Enjoy an elegant dinner while Professor Johnson shares insights from his Nobel Prize-winning work, reflects on his experience in Stockholm, and explores how artificial intelligence and economic policy are shaping our future. Launching the MIT Endicott House Nobel Laureate Series, this inaugural dinner offers a rare opportunity to engage with one of MIT's Nobel laureates in an intimate setting. Guests will enjoy exceptional cuisine, thoughtful conversation, and insights rarely shared outside the world's leading academic institutions.

title: Anooradha Iyer Siddiqi and Rachel Lee
description: Anooradha Iyer Siddiqi and Rachel Lee Presented with the HTC Forum Part of the MIT Fall 2026 Architecture Lecture Series The Work of Collaboration Collaboration has often occupied an ambiguous place within architectural history, a discipline that continues to privilege individual authorship, singular expertise and archival authority. Collaboration can unsettle these privileges. By bringing researchers together it reshapes the questions we ask, the evidence we value and the histories we are able to write. Taking the Feminist Architectural Histories of Migration project as a point of departure, we reflect on collaboration as both a feminist practice and a mode of historical inquiry. Drawing on our shared work, as well as subsequent projects developed with artists, designers, archivists, communities and fellow researchers, we consider how collaborative methods have transformed our scholarship. Rather than presenting collaboration as an exception to scholarly practice, the lecture argues that it is a way of producing more generous, situated and critically engaged architectural histories. Looking back at one collaboration and forward to many others, it asks what kinds of historical knowledge become possible when research is understood as a collective endeavour. Rachel Lee Rachel Lee is Assistant Professor in the Department of Architecture at TU Delft. Her research explores colonial and postcolonial architecture and urbanism, migration, gender and heritage, with a particular interest in how architectural histories are researched, written and shared through archives, collaboration and material culture. Her work spans archival research, oral history, exhibitions and digital publishing, developing collaborative approaches to architectural history. Her work includes Feminist Architectural Histories of Migration, a long-term collaboration with architectural historian Anooradha Siddiqi; Planted!, a collaborative digital archive tracing the global histories of a colonial chair;

title: A Closer Look at Charley Longfellow’s “Japan Room"
description: Charles Appleton Longfellow (1844–1893), the eldest son of poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow and Frances Appleton Longfellow, was a globetrotter and avid collector. During his 20-month stay in Japan (1871–1873), he purchased and shipped home to Cambridge dozens of crates of artworks and decorative objects for himself, friends, and family. Upon his return in 1874, Charley transformed the sitting room at his family home into a “Japan Room” with the help of his cousin Alexander Wadsworth Longfellow (1854–1934). One of its most striking features was a ceiling decorated with more than 35 fan-shaped paintings arranged in a “scattered fan” pattern. Although Japanese art and decorative objects had entered U.S. markets by the mid-1870s, their availability and visibility varied considerably by city. Created in 1874, on the eve of the transformative 1876 Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia, the Japan Room represents an unusually early American domestic interior devoted to Japanese art and design. This lecture examines its remarkable ceiling of fan paintings, exploring their origins and arrangement and considering how this distinctive feature of the room reflects the ways Japanese art was displayed and experienced in nineteenth-century America. This research was supported by the Friends of the Longfellow House-Washington's Headquarters 2025 Art Research Fellowship Program. ————————————— Elizabeth K. Sackler Gallery), and the Anacostia Community Museum. Her museum career has also included positions at the Walters Art Museum, the National Gallery of Art, and the American Alliance of Museums. title: CPL Presents America Unfinished: 250 Years of Law and Governance (Main)
description: Join editors Alexandra Natapoff and Guy-Uriel Charles, along with contributors to America Unfinished: 250 Years of Law and Governance, for a discussion of this new collection of essays marking America’s 250th anniversary. America Unfinished brings together more than 50 legal scholars from the Harvard Law School faculty to examine a pivotal moment in American law and governance. The collection’s 62 essays explore topics including the expansion of executive power, the relationship between workers, consumers, and markets, democratic accountability in a market-driven economy, and the future of knowledge and governance institutions amid rapid technological change. Contributors include Stephen Breyer, Tomiko Brown-Nagin, Noah Feldman, Annette Gordon-Reed, Randall Kennedy, Jill Lepore, Lawrence Lessig, Bruce H. Mann, Martha Minow, and Cass R. Sunstein. title: ChemE Dept. Seminar: New Perspectives on Large Amplitude Oscillatory Shear Rheology
description: Speaker: Joseph Peterson, Assistant Professor of Chemical and Biomedical Engineering; UCLA Large Amplitude Oscillatory Shear flows (LAOS) provide a versatile and reproducible means of measuring a material's response to unsteady and nonlinear flow conditions, which are typical of real processing conditions. But interpreting LAOS measurements remains a challenge, and foundational assumptions - such as a linear velocity field - may not even be correct. In this talk, we will investigate the linear response function of LAOS flows for highly entangled and shear thinning polymer melts, and build connections to disparate fields including quantum mechanics and process controls. The first part of the talk will focus on developing a new experimental and mathematical analysis framework for parallel superposition rheology in LAOS, uncovering a general stability criterion for shear banding instabilities. The second part of the talk extends the discussion to two dimensional flows, following the linear stability of Kelvin waves and the subsequent nonlinear dynamics in two dimensional LAOS flows.

description: Students can expect a high-energy, joyful African and Caribbean dance-fitness experience that combines easy-to-follow choreography, rhythmic movement, cardio, and culturally inspired dance styles. The class is designed for all levels, from beginners to experienced dancers, with modifications and repetition that allow everyone to participate at their own pace. Sylver’s teaching philosophy is rooted in creating a welcoming, judgment-free environment where students can connect with the music, move freely, build confidence, and have fun while getting a great workout. African and Caribbean dance traditions are rooted in the diverse cultures of countries such as Madagascar, Senegal, Ghana, Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Haiti, Jamaica, Trinidad & Tobago, and Cuba, among many others. The movement and rhythms represented in ’Froca Fitness draw inspiration from forms such as Malagasy dance, Sabar, Azonto, Kizomba, Coupé-Décalé, Ndombolo, Afrobeats, Dancehall, Soca, Kompa, and traditional Haitian rhythms, reflecting generations of African and Caribbean cultural expression, resilience, and exchange. ’Froca Fitness honors this legacy by bringing these influences into a contemporary, high-energy dance-fitness experience that celebrates the diversity and global impact of Afro-diasporic movement and music. title: Beginner and Intermediate Tap for All Levels
description: Classes teach Broadway style tap and focus on repetitive technique to encourage muscle memory and the confidence to create clear sounds. Inclusion is a priority so that all students feel welcome. Classes are “drop-in”, meaning you may join any week and there’s no “semester” commitment. Past steps are always reviewed with the introduction of 1 or 2 new steps or combos each class. Similar to a yoga class, students work at their own individual levels and build up skill at their own pace. Beginners will feel comfortable regardless of when they join. Cost: $20 for 1 hour | $25 for 90 minutes *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. Registration: Email or text Christina Harrington to register: charrington9901@gmail.com | (617) 852-6240 Pre-registration is encouraged but not required. Drop-ins are welcome. Accepted Payments: Cash, Venmo (@christina-harrington-7) What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Tap dancing began as an answer to the horrors of colonial enslavement…with no musical instruments, Irish and West African slaves turned to their own feet to create rhythms and percussion while pulling movement and technique from traditional tribal and cultural dances. Sounds were initially made with wooden soles, then pennies and bottle caps, finally becoming the modern metal plates screwed to the ball and heel of the shoes. These dances made their way to minstrel and vaudeville shows, eventually transforming into the broadway and rhythm style tap dancing we know today. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? Christina Harrington joined The Dance Complex as a Teaching Artist in May 2012. title: Soul Dance – An Embodied Movement Practice
description: A guided improvisational movement practice that engages somatic awareness to facilitate personal growth, emotional well-being, and collective healing. Welcoming participants of all experience levels, bodies and identities. We dance to expand and evolve our embodiment. We dance to release stored tension, emotions and patterns. We dance to integrate our experiences and we dance to remember who we really are. We enter in a cycle of movement that begins slow, builds in intensity, peaks, lightens, and then settles. Through verbal instructions, participants are invited to explore, in their own bodies way – a variety of movement patterns, physical inquiries, and focal points. The journey is curated to an intentional and eclectic world music soundscape. It is a journey where you might sweat (though you are always in control of your rhythm and pace).This class allows you to engage with the wisdom of your own body, to take you on a journey. Some of which include, improvisational authentic-movement, physical theatre, somatic therapy, dance-movement choreography- highly influenced by Pina Bausch-, ancient practices, shamanic study, yogic, buddhist and influences from my own artistic and spiritual path of healing. One of the most remarkable things about this class is the vast range of participants, in terms of age, dance experience, and connections to Haiti. title: Samba & Afro-Brazilian
description: The main goal of our class is to have fun and feel the joy of movement and expression. We also strive to build technical competence and an appreciation for Brazilian culture through music and dance. We start with a warm-up, work on technique and styling, and often learn a short combo. Samba is a rhythm and a dance that exudes equal parts beauty, spirituality, and resistance. Borne in Brazil from enslaved Africans, samba has spread to the mainstream and is now one of the country’s most famous exports. Samba is constantly evolving in all of its forms; currently there are many popular samba sub-genres, including pagode, samba rock, bossa nova, etc. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? SambaViva teachers have a minimum of 5 (and as many as 20!) years dancing and training samba and other Brazilian styles. All have trained closely with Brazilian instructors both intensively and over many years. Our regular instructors have traveled extensively in the country to study dance but also to participate in the culture, learn the language, and explore the many sites and experiences Brazil has to offer. title: The Getaway Driver
description: Based on the true story of Katherine Ann Power and Clare Schroeder, this gripping new drama follows two women bound by a single, life-altering moment. It’s 1970. College student Power joins an activist group to protest the war. When their resistance turns deadly, Schroeder must grow up in the shadow of her father’s murder while Power disappears and spends decades on the FBI’s Most Wanted List. Years later, when Power resurfaces seeking redemption, she must confront Schroeder and the past that shaped their lives. Unfolding like a true crime thriller, this remarkable story asks: How far is too far in the fight to do what’s right?

title: Stems & Sips: Sake & Ikebana
description: Saturday, October 31, 6:30-8:00pm EST Find your flow, one branch and one pour at a time. True harmony happens when you strip things down to their absolute essence. In Japan, this philosophy connects two beautiful crafts: Ikebana (minimalist floral arrangement) and Sake (the refined art of brewing). Join us for Stems & Sips, a relaxed, hands-on evening designed for beginners. No complex jargon, no overwhelming flower bundles—just clean flavors, striking lines, and a healthy dose of fun. What to Expect Sake Demystified: Discover the stunning versatility of premium sake. You’ll taste a curated flight—ranging from bright and fruity to crisp and earthy—while learning the basics of how it’s made and served. The Living Sculpture: Dive into Ikebana, the traditional art of flower arrangement. Unlike dense Western bouquets, Ikebana focuses on negative space, asymmetry, and making a few thoughtful stems speak volumes. Guided Creation: We will walk you through the core principles of line, depth, and form. Step-by-step, you’ll learn how to position branches and blossoms to mimic the grace of nature. No experience required. We provide the tools, the knowledge, and the liquid inspiration. You’ll leave with a gorgeous centerpiece, a newfound appreciation for Japanese craft, and a serious sense of zen. description: Know Before You Go How to join: Check in at the Visitor Services desk; space is limited. Fee: This is a free event. Accessibility accommodations: If you would like to request accommodations for your visit, please contact Visitor Services at am_register@harvard.edu or 617-495-9400. For more details about accommodations at the museums, please see the Accessibility page. General info: The museum visit page has general guidelines for your visit. On this tour, Jide Anekwe ‘28 will look at the significance of color in the ancient Mediterranean world and at modern perceptions of the past. The stops on the tour are: Portrait of a woman, a painting from Roman Imperial Egypt (c. 130–150 CE); Youthful hero or god, a marble sculpture from Imperial Rome (1st–2nd century CE) after a Greek sculpture by Skopas from the fourth century BCE; and William Holman Hunt’s painting The Miracle of the Sacred Fire, Church of the Holy Sepulchre (1892–99). Spotlight Tours are designed and led by Harvard undergraduates from a range of academic disciplines. Each tour is focused on objects chosen by the student and provides visitors a unique, thematic view into the collections. Tours typically feature three works of art, embrace a conversational format, and last about 45 minutes. Open to the public, these tours start outside the museum shop on Saturdays and Sundays at 11am and 2pm. This program is supported by the Ho Family Student Guide Fund. The Ho Family Student Guide Program at the Harvard Art Museums prepares students to develop original, research-based tours. Through their training, Student Guides gain knowledge of the collections and develop skills in critical thinking, visual analysis, public speaking, and leadership. Find out what the Student Guides are up to anytime on Instagram @harvardarthappens.

title: Community Science Fair
description: Join us for Mount Auburn’s Community Science Fair, where biodiversity research leaders will share their work at interactive stations inside Bigelow Chapel. Attendees will have the chance to meet local experts, learn about ongoing projects, and discover how to get involved in supporting urban ecology. As one of the largest green spaces in the area, Mount Auburn is home to a wide range of species. But urbanization and climate change threaten wildlife through habitat loss, fragmentation, and pollution. In response, we are working to improve habitat, increase both plant and animal diversity, and monitor the many species that visit and reside on our grounds. Through partnerships with local scientists, Mount Auburn conducts 18 ongoing observation-based field projects and offers a citizen science naturalist program that trains volunteers to support biodiversity research. From classroom education to field training, these programs connect people with the natural world while helping us collect vital data on native flora and fauna. Come learn how Mount Auburn balances the built and the wild environments within the city—and how you can be part of our efforts to sustain a healthy, thriving landscape for generations to come. title: Multispecies Warfare in Palestine-Israel: A talk by Irus Braverman
description: Brook Farm Institute for Critical Studies welcomes Radcliffe scholar Irus Braverman as the next speaker in our ongoing public lecture series, Critical Interventions. Animals have long played important roles in human warfare. Drawing on ethnographic research and on her own experiences growing up in Palestine-Israel, Braverman will explore how nonhuman animals have become active participants in Israeli warfare and how warfare itself has been shaped by their presence. Introducing the concept of “multispecies warfare,” she will show that animals are not simply instruments of military violence, but that they also acquire political significance through animal welfare regulations, animal rights initiatives, property regimes, and environmental protections. Sheep seize territory through grazing, dogs become subjects of rescue and humanization, donkeys sustain mobility under siege, crocodiles operate as imagined security technologies, and camel movement becomes criminalized through conservation laws. Warfare, then, is enacted through both violence and care. By tracing unexpected connections between humans, animals, and war, Braverman will offer a new way of thinking about warfare itself: not as an exclusively human endeavor, but as a complex multispecies project that shapes political worlds.

title: Inheritance: A Litany
description: “Inheritance: A Litany” is a deeply intimate, yet universal, personal narrative, dance-opera-play, and comic drama created and performed by Janis Brenner. Inspired by Ms. Brenner’s late parents, the 51-minute work is a journey into the myriad of ways Ms. Brenner “became” her parents—inheriting her father’s wavy hair and sarcasm, her mother’s singing voice and fragile bones. The autobiographical one-woman show reveals aspects of a family’s story, as well as the nature of how we become who we are. The interdisciplinary tour-de-force also uncovers what make us each unique, complicated, and fragile human beings. This show is appropriate for ages 14 and up. “We need artists like Ms. Brenner now in this world, as she crosses genres, asks hard questions, and brings a gentleness and tenderness to her rendering of parents who were equal parts loving and exasperating, protecting and needy, known and misunderstood. We emerge emboldened, ready to create our own litanies, ready for family voices to speak.” – Cynthia Darling, All About Solo, 2019 JANIS BRENNER: Janis Brenner is a renowned, multi-award-winning dancer/choreographer/singer/teacher, and Artistic Director of Janis Brenner & Dancers in NYC. Honors include: “Bessie” Award in Meredith Monk’s “The Politics of Quiet”, Lester Horton Award in L.A., Fund for US Artists at International Festivals, U.S. State Department, Asian Cultural Council, The Trust for Mutual Understanding, US Embassies in Moscow, Bosnia, Jakarta and Dakar, O’Donnell Green Music and Dance Foundation (multiple grants) and a commission from the Whitney Museum of American Art for “The Memory Project.” Her work has been commissioned/re-staged on more than 55 companies and colleges worldwide. Brenner worked closely for years with Meredith Monk & Vocal Ensemble, Michael Moschen, Annabelle Gamson, and with Murray Louis Dance Company, Bat Sheva Dance Company and Alwin Nikolais. title: Monday Moments for Friends, Fellows, and Partners
description: We invite Friends, Fellows, and Partners of the museums to explore two fascinating exhibitions at their own pace through a self-guided visit: On Location: Drawing the Outdoors (September 18, 2026–January 17, 2027) and The Way We Never Were: The American Professional Photographers Collection (August 29, 2026–May 9, 2027). In the exhibition On Location: Drawing the Outdoors, discover how an intimate relationship with nature shaped the artistic vision of 19th-century European artists. Featuring approximately 140 sketches, watercolors, and pastels by artists including J. M. W. Turner, Berthe Morisot, Paul Cézanne, and Vincent van Gogh, the exhibition is organized as a series of thematic journeys through the landscape and explores changing ideas about nature, environmental awareness, and artistic identity. It invites visitors to reflect on why these artists’ experiences of the outdoors continue to resonate today. The Way We Never Were explores how professional photography helped shape Americans’ understanding of life after World War II. Drawn from the Harvard Art Museums’ American Professional Photographers Collection, the exhibition features commissioned photographs of weddings, schools, businesses, and other everyday moments that presented an idealized vision of postwar America. These images not only documented the era but also influenced cultural memory by highlighting certain experiences while leaving others out. Through themes of prosperity, suburbia, conformity, and the struggle for equal rights, the exhibition encourages visitors to reconsider the story these photographs tell about the American past. This special preview is our way of thanking you for your support and dedication to the Harvard Art Museums. To become a Friend, Fellow, or Partner, please visit our Support page. title: Rachel Dorothy Tanur Memorial Lecture: Pneuhaus “Building with Air”
description: Pneuhaus began by blowing bubbles: a joint thesis project built around a fascination with inflatables and what could be made of them at a craft level. This talk traces how that early curiosity grew into a full-fledged art, design, and fabrication studio. Working hands-on with materials and techniques eventually shaped an unusual business model, closer to a traveling circus than a design studio, where work packs down small, travels light, and can go up almost anywhere in the world. August Lehrecke, Pneuhaus co-founder, will cover how making and installing their work built the studio Pneuhaus runs today, and how commissioned projects sharpen the skills and tools they carry back into the creative practice. Underneath it all is a fascination with how much a shift in air pressure can change: soft turns rigid, a surface lets light through or blocks it out, or a structure deforms underfoot. Lehrecke will discuss various studio projects and the areas the studio is currently exploring.

title: Deni Elliott at Harvard Book Store
description: Harvard Book Store welcomes Deni Elliott —co-director for the National Ethics Project and professor emerita in the Department of Journalism and Digital Communication at the University of South Florida—for a discussion of her new book, Catching Sight: How a Guide Dog Helped Me See Myself. About Catching Sight One woman’s journey through progressive blindness and the extraordinary guide dog who kept her safe along the way. When ethics scholar Deni Elliott, born with limited vision, realized she could no longer navigate the world safely alone, she turned to a guide dog—a decision that reshaped her understanding of disability and independence. Written in collaboration with master trainer Graham Buck, Catching Sight offers a behind-the-scenes look at the world of guide dog breeding and training, revealing the intelligence and decision-making skills these dogs develop from birth. Catching Sight is for readers interested in the transformative power of human relationships with animals. As Deni confronts her changing reality, she shares the hidden world of guide dog training and introduces Alberta, a yellow Lab whose quiet brilliance changed her interaction with the world and herself. Catching Sight offers a fresh and unforgettable perspective on disability, identity, and the power of partnership.

title: Jerry Bergonzi Quartet
description: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 8:30 start / 8pm doors / seated Jerry Bergonzi , Tenor Saxophone Luther Gray , Drums Special Guest , Trumpet Special Guest , Bass A fine, high-powered tenor saxophonist with a tone influenced by John Coltrane, a mastery of chord changes, and a strong musical imagination, Jerry Bergonzi has long had an underground following in the Boston area. He started on clarinet when he was eight, switching to alto at 12, and finally to tenor two years later. Bergonzi was inspired early on by Sonny Rollins, Coltrane, and Hank Mobley. He attended Lowell University and then after graduation played electric bass in local bands behind singers and strippers, saving up enough money to move to New York in 1972. After struggling in the Big Apple for seven years and gaining some recognition as a member of Two Generations of Brubeck and of the Dave Brubeck Quartet (with whom he appeared on several Concord albums during 1979-1981), Bergonzi moved back to Boston in 1981, where he developed a strong career both as a tenorman and as an educator. He has since led several groups (including two called Con Brio and Gonz) and recorded for the Plug, Not Fat, Red, and Blue Note labels. — By Scott Yanow, AllMusic Continuing Every Monday at 8:30pm Lineup subject to change

Bassist Appleman left the band in 1985 to become Chairman of the Bass Department at Berklee College and was replaced by veteran bassist John Lockwood . Bob Gullotti passed away in 2020 and is remembered as one of the greatest jazz drummers of his generation. Francisco Mela, now on drums, graciously fills the space Bob left behind. Along with their impressive tenure with The Fringe, Garzone, Lockwood, and Mela are in great demand as session players and have played with many of the greats of contemporary jazz. Along with keeping up with a busy performance schedule, each of them are well-respected educators helping to inspire the jazz musicians of tomorrow. title: Online Seminar On Undergraduate Mathematics Education
description: Speaker:Rebecca Swanson (Colorado School of Mines) Title: Lessons from Flipped Classrooms: Implementing Partially and Fully Flipped Learning Across the Mathematics Curriculum Abstract: Flipped learning is often presented as an all-or-nothing instructional choice, which can make it feel inaccessible or risky—especially in content-heavy mathematics courses. In this talk, I share my lessons from 10+ years of experience implementing both fully flipped and partially flipped models across a range of mathematics courses at the Colorado School of Mines, including Calculus II, Linear Algebra, Foundations of Advanced Mathematics, and Topology. I discuss how different flipping choices supported student learning, how the model scales to multi-section courses, and how I addressed some of the challenges that emerged. Rather than advocating for a single model, this talk emphasizes intentional, flexible flipping strategies that can be adapted to instructors’ own goals and constraints. Students continue center work and stretching as they progress in strength and musicality. Students can register for one, two, or all three classes! Girls’ Dress Code: Solid-Color Leotard, Ballet Pink or Skin Tone Footed Tights, Pink or Skin Tone Canvas Ballet Slippers. Ballet skirts and warm-ups are not permitted. Hair must be neatly secured in a bun away from the face and neck. Boys’ Dress Code: White T-Shirt, Black Tights or Leggings, Black Ballet Slippers. Hair must be neatly secured away from the face and neck. Age 8 by 09/01/26 REGISTER HERE *Tuition price includes the registration fee and The Dance Complex Youth Membership What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? The School of Classical Ballet was founded in 1985 by Anna Myer and Patricia Adelmann. For over 30 years, the school has provided students with classical ballet training and helped to develop student appreciation for dance as an art form. We currently offer classes in ballet and contemporary. Director Kirsta Sendziak, faculty, and staff continue to provide students the quality of instruction upon which the school was founded. The School of Classical Ballet is a technique-based school with emphasis on learning. Performances are all-inclusive for students to showcase their technique and gain experience performing for an audience. title: The Art & Technique of Isadora Duncan: for 8-11 year olds
description: Rainbowdance® prepares children aged 5-18 for this program. Having an established sense of harmony & affiliation to each other & to the natural world, they move forward to explore their unique & collective beauty & expression. Children explore emotional intention, manifested through music & movement. Themes include: Leadership & Following, Join & Retreat, Transition, Alone & together, Nature as Teacher, Myth Based Dances & Improv. Dancers with special needs are always welcome. We will work with you to find the right class & offer 1:1 sessions when appropriate. Cost: $240 for 15 Classes | $225 Sibling Rate Please register with Boston Children’s Foundation. Class sizes are limited and filled upon receipt of tuition. If classes are at capacity upon registration, you will be placed on a waitlist: REGISTER HERE Accepted Payments: Cash, Check, PayPal What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? The Art & Technique of Isadora Duncan offers celebratory explorations of relationship to classical music, peers, ancestral community & nature. Duncan, “Mother of Modern Dance,” sought movements expressive of the human spirit; her technique glorifies natural movement, sources rhythmic & emotional links fundamental to all life & traces dance to its sacred roots using mythological archetypes & ritual. Dicki has for 30+yrs encourage responsiveness to beautiful music & joyful movements inspired by nature in non-competitive environments for healthy emotional, creative & physical development. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? Dicki, a 3rd generation Duncan Dancer, was trained as a child by Anita Zahn (Isadora’s student). She carries on the tradition which informs her Rainbowdance® program, & her training of graduate students. Duncan Dance classes for teens (age 12+) and adults, offer a non-competitive environment designed to encourage and sustain healthy emotional, creative, and physical relationships. She carries on the tradition which informs her Rainbowdance® program, & her training of graduate students. She is an Isadora Duncan Movement Analyst, director of the performance group Guardians of Isadora, BC-DMT, LMHC, and the director of Boston Children’s Foundation (BCF). title: Mat Pilates with Carolina Laredo
description: 60 min Mat Pilates class using the Tabata method. We break down movements to really understand our bodies and find connection. Mat Pilates focuses on core strength and the rejuvenation of the body through micro movements. Pilates was created in similar concepts to physical therapy; to heal the body with safe movement. One hour of fun music and a workout that will leave you smiling, strong and empowered. Accessible and inclusive to all bodies. Students should bring their own water bottle and mat. Cost: $15 Single Class *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership or a $5 Day Pass to access the building. REGISTER HERE Accepted Payments: Sign up via website or pay in person: cash, Venmo, Paypal, Cashapp What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Mat Pilates is a low-impact exercise that uses body weight to strengthen and lengthen the body, particularly the core. It’s based on the original exercises created by Joseph Pilates, and can be practiced on a mat with little to no equipment. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? Carolina started her journey teaching in 2020. She has always been an active person participating in track, playing soccer, biking, and bouldering. In 2018 she started to take yoga classes and Pilates classes. She fell in love with movement once again. when the pandemic hit she did her first certification for Mat Pilates, then soon after also got certified in strength classes, 300 hour training in Hot 26 yoga, 100 hours of Trauma informed yoga, and Yin yoga training. Carolina’s certifications all align in how she teaches her classes that are mindful and invigorating. title: Street Jazz
description: Patrick has a way of giving students the confidence and skills to stand out in an audition, at the club, or just in life. This class will help you develop technique, a strong stage presence, and an athlete’s body & mindset. Patrick’s warm up consists of various stretches, push-ups, crunches, and club moves – overall building up your cardiovascular stamina and strength. Cost: $25.00 Single Class | Package pricing available at patplanet.com *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. REGISTER HERE Accepted Payments: Cash, Venmo (@pat-planet), PayPal, or sign up via patplanet.com What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Street Jazz is a commercial-dance style seen in mainstream entertainment including music videos, concerts, tours, and movies by many of your favorite pop stars. We’ll dive into various street styles, from Hip-Hop to Funk and beyond, blending them with the sharp lines and precision found in a Jazz class. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? Patrick is a choreographer, educator, and performer with credits spanning stage, film, and sports arenas. His credits include Sony Music, Red Bull, Epic Records, Law & Order, BLOCH, Britney Spears, TEDx, Macy’s, Whitney Houston: I Wanna Dance with Somebody (2022), AMF, and more. He has served as university faculty at The Boston Conservatory, Pennsylvania State University, and Endicott College. In 2022, Patrick debuted as the first male NBA Celtics Dancer in history; since then, he has collaborated with the NFL Patriots Cheerleaders, has choreographed for local artists, and worked with sports-entertainment dance teams. Patrick is a Certified Dance Coach with the Universal Dance Association (UDA). title: Musical Theater Dance with Ramone Owens
description: This class is designed for students that want to enhance technical proficiency and performance in Musical Theater dance and Jazz. It is designed to expand and finesse the relationship with music and space— exploring movement and musicality through Jazz and Musical Theater styles. This class highlights artistic expression, improvisation, storytelling and choreography. Step into a dynamic Broadway-style dance class designed to sharpen your technique and strengthen your performance. Come ready to move, take risks, make bold choices, and HAVE FUN! Cost: $20 for single class *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. REGISTER HERE What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Broadway- style is steeped in the traditions of American Jazz dance–which emerged from African American movement and musical practices while drawing from ballet, tap, vaudeville, modern and various cultural traditions. The form brings together many lineages into conversation through musicality, character, storytelling and expressive movement. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? Ramone Owens’s relationship with musical theater dance began through his formal training at Boston Conservatory, where he earned a B.F.A. in Musical Theater. He deepened that training through more than a decade as a professional performer, including *Motown the Musical* on Broadway and national tour and the original Broadway company of *Beetlejuice*. Now a director, choreographer, and Assistant Professor of Theater at Boston Conservatory at Berklee, he approaches the form from both artistic and pedagogical perspectives. His teaching draws upon his experience in the classroom, rehearsal room, and on the Broadway stage to help dancers integrate technique, musicality, character, and storytelling. title: Capoeira MdP
description: Students can expect a welcoming and engaging class that brings together Capoeira’s movement, music, rhythm, self-defense, and cultural traditions. Classes are designed for all levels, combining physical training and creativity in an environment centered on respect, community, and individual growth. Students are also introduced to traditions such as Maculelê and Samba, offering a broader experience of the culture surrounding Capoeira. Cost: Drop-In Class – $25 | 10 Class Pack (Valid for 60 days) – $175 More information available through the registration link *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. REGISTER HERE Accepted Payments: Cash, Venmo (@capoeiramdp), Zelle (contact@capoeiramdp.com), Credit Card through Registration Platform – 4% fee added to any purchase made through Venmo/Credit Card What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Capoeira is an Afro-Brazilian art form developed in Brazil by enslaved Africans and their descendants, bringing together elements of martial arts, movement, music, and cultural expression. We teach Capoeira Contemporânea, which draws from the traditions of both Capoeira Regional and Capoeira Angola while incorporating influences that have developed throughout Brazil. This style reflects Capoeira’s continued evolution while maintaining a strong connection to its history and cultural roots. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? With over 50 years of continuous Capoeira practice and more than 40 years of teaching experience, I founded Associação de Capoeira Mandingueiros dos Palmares (Capoeira MdP) in 1977 in Belo Horizonte, Brazil. Our practice of Capoeira Contemporânea is deeply rooted in the traditions of Capoeira Regional developed by Mestre Bimba. title: Kathak Foundations
description: Come with an open mind, in comfortable, modest clothing that doesn’t cover your feet, hair tied back, and ready to move from your head to your toes, inside and out! Learn how we make rhythms with different parts of our feet, use our voices to create vibrations, rhythms and melodies that complement our dance and how we bring in hand gestures and expression to build compositions and even stories! You will build focus, strength, stamina, and creativity as we move together and experience a unique sense of and perspective on holistic wellness. We are fortunate to have regular tabla accompaniment by master drummer, Akili Jamal Haynes, which only enhances the experience as your body and mind connect with the rhythms. Simply come experience all the dance has to offer YOU uniquely. It’s meant for anyone and everyone. Cost: $25.00 Single Class | $88 for 4-Class Pass | $147 for 7-Class Pass | $20 per class for full session (prorated) For 2+ classes per week the fee is $35 per week. *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. REGISTER HERE Accepted Payments: Cash, Check, Venmo (@Anjali-Nath-2), Zelle (3711) What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Anjali teaches in the unique style of Pandit Chitresh Das, founded in the Lucknow Gharana (style) with influence of the Jaipur Gharana along with a technique he developed called Kathak Yoga, where you will learn how we can integrate multiple rhythms through our dance. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? My kathak journey began with Gretchen Hayden, Founder of Chhandika Boston and Senior Disciple of Pandit Chitresh Das. Pandit Das was the pioneer of kathak dance bringing his rich training and upbringing in Kolkata, India to the US in 1971. title: Free Comedy Open-Mic
description: 18+ w/ Suggested 2-Item Minimum. Door   List at 6pm. Free Show. No Ticket Needed.The Globe described the night as “Comedy Hell” when we were upstairs in Somerville’s Union Square. Now we’re two floors down in a basement in Cambridge’s Harvard Square, under where the first and last Curious George shop died. It’s even better. Enter our comedy world, whether you listen, laugh, bomb, groan, clap or just sip your beverage with a raised eyebrow… We just LOVE it. It’s an Open Mic, but there’s always some pros dropping in to test new material, so it’s unavoidable to have a good time, for free no less. Doors and list open at 6 pm. The heat starts around 7 pm. The Bar Our Bar opens 1 hour before early shows and 20 minutes before late shows. So come early and grab a drink with us! The Bar also stays open until 1 AM, so stop by after our last show of the evening! **No outside food or beverages allowed**

title: Defy the Dusk Release Bash with Danielle L. Jensen
description: Gather round at First Parish for a release-day celebration of #1 New York Times bestselling author, Danielle L. Jensen’s latest release! Defy the Dusk: Book One of The Sundering Duet is a gritty post-apocalyptic fantasy duology. Hear Danielle in conversation with #1 New York Times bestselling author Elise Kova about creating the story of the Sundered world, where there are two options: ride the dawn, or face what rises in the night. When darkness means certain death and survival depends on reaching the dawn, the woman whose magic broke the world will carve another path: defy the dusk. Be the first to get your hands on this stunning first edition hardcover featuring designed sprayed edges and endpapers, a custom foil-stamped case, and a deluxe jacket with foil at the day-of-release celebration. Tickets include a pre-signed copy of Defy the Dusk that Danielle has offered to personalize during your meet and greet. In addition to one personalization, the author will sign up to one backlist title purchased during the event or brought from home. Each book comes with special bonus art prints! 6:30 PM: Doors Open – Grab your pre-signed copy of Defy the Dusk, settle in, and get ready for a great discussion! 7:00 PM: Discussion Begins – Danielle will dive into Defy the Dusk. 7:45 PM: Q&A Session – Your chance to ask the author anything! 9:00 PM: Event Wraps Up – Thanks for joining us!

title: Beginner/Intermediate Flamenco with Nino de los Reyes
description: Students can expect to learn flamenco from the roots and it’s tradition. We will work on technique, choreography (that will be performed by the end of the semester) and they will learn flamenco codes which are very important to be able to really understand the art form. title: The Picower Institute Fall 2026 Symposium "Comparative Neuroscience: Lessons from Biodiversity"
description: The Picower Institute Fall 2026 Symposium "Comparative Neuroscience: Lessons from Biodiversity" Date: Wednesday, November 4, 2026Time: 9:00am-5:00pmLocation: Singleton Auditorium (46-3002, Third Fl of MIT Building 46)Address: 43 Vassar Street, Cambridge, MA 02139Faculty Host: Brady WeissbourdRegistration: Free but required. Click here to register. Please Note: This event is in-person only. Animal behavior is incredibly diverse, from insect to human societies; from jellyfish jet propulsion to flying bats. This symposium will bring together scientists with distinct perspectives to examine how nervous systems are organized across species and how these organizational principles relate to mechanisms of nervous system evolution. We will explore questions such as: to what extent do diverse nervous systems share common principles, and when they do, why? What can we learn from species differences? - for example, why are some brains more regenerative than others? How does evolution alter the nervous system to generate novel behaviors? - and how do we compare neural networks across species and levels of complexity to ask such questions? With speakers ranging from evolutionary biology to computational neuroscience, we expect this to be an exciting and thought-provoking day of science. Speakers Herwig Baier, Max Planck Institute for Biological IntelligenceAdrienne Fairhall, University of WashingtonOliver Hobert, HHMI, Columbia UniversityDaniel Kronauer, HHMI, The Rockefeller UniversityKanaka Rajan, Harvard UniversityVanessa Ruta, The Rockefeller UniversityAlejandro Sánchez Alvarado, Stowers Institute for Medical ResearchElly Tanaka, IMBA - Institute of Molecular BiotechnologyMichael Yartsev, HHMI, UC Berkeley

Developed in response to gaps in traditional health and wellness systems, Majestic Healing Pathways™ centers the lived experiences of Black and Brown communities who face disproportionate stress, trauma, and barriers to care. The model honors the reality that healing is not a single intervention, but a pathway built over time through breath, movement, rest, relationship, and choice. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? For more than 20 years, Nora has been teaching yoga and dance to students of all ages. title: Intermediate/Advanced Ballet with Dean Vollick
description: Class begins with a thorough set of exercises at the barre that last from 30 to 45 minutes. Centre practice follows, and may consist of a battement tendu exercise, a battement jeté exercise, a grand battement exercise, small and/or large adage, stationary turns, traveling turns, and petite and grand allegro enchaînement (small and big jumps). Classes are structured so that the dancer warms up their feet, legs, hips and upper body gradually. As class progresses there are more changes of weight and eventually, sudden changes of direction. Live music is provided by a pianist, that ranges from classical pieces to selections from ballet repertoire to improvisational contemporary music. Cost: $20 Single Class | $15.00 barre | 5-class package $90.00 *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. Please register in studio with the class assistant Accepted Payments: Cash, Check, Venmo What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Ballet originated in the Italian Renaissance courts around 1500 as large balls or spectacles that were performed by members of the royal court. The French king, Louis XIV, created the first academy and the positions, steps, and movements of the ballet were collected and codified. The spectacles began to be performed by artists that were trained in the academy, originally as part of an opera, and later as ballets that told a story through music, mime, and dance. Over the centuries ballet has influenced folk dance styles of many (mainly European) nations and, more recently, has been influenced by folk, modern, and contemporary forms of dance from all countries. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I had a professional dance career that spanned more than twenty years and included company work in both ballet and contemporary companies as well as dancing, choreographing, and teaching as a freelance artist.

description: Rainbowdance® prepares children aged 5-18 for this program. Having an established sense of harmony & affiliation to each other & to the natural world, they move forward to explore their unique & collective beauty & expression. The Art & Technique of Isadora Duncan offers celebratory explorations of relationship to classical music, peers, ancestral community & nature. Duncan, “Mother of Modern Dance,” sought movements expressive of the human spirit; her technique glorifies natural movement, sources rhythmic & emotional links fundamental to all life & traces dance to its sacred roots using mythological archetypes & ritual. Dicki has for 30+yrs encourage responsiveness to beautiful music & joyful movements inspired by nature in non-competitive environments for healthy emotional, creative & physical development. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? Dicki, a 3rd generation Duncan Dancer, was trained as a child by Anita Zahn (Isadora’s student). She carries on the tradition which informs her Rainbowdance® program, & her training of graduate students. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? Yu-Ling founded Yuling Spanish Dance in 2017 and she has been offering Flamenco classes and performances. Yu-Ling is also a board certified Dance/Movement Therapist and she offers The Discipline of Authentic Moment practice. title: Artist Talk: Enzo Camacho and Ami Lien
description: The 2026 Nancy Stephenson Nichols Memorial Lecture Join visual artists and Harvard alumni Enzo Camacho (A.B. ’07) and Ami Lien (A.B. ’09) as they share insights and developments into their practice as artistic collaborators. Working between New York, Berlin, and Manila, Camacho and Lien develop research-based, site-specific, and documentary projects to examine histories of labor, land, and resistance in the Philippines. Their research on the enduring influence of Alfonso Ossorio’s mural commission at the Chapel of St. Joseph the Worker on Negros Island has led them to investigate the sugar plantation landscape that grounds this historic site-specific artwork. In their ongoing engagement with Negros Island, the artists focus on the defiant forms of culture-making that emerge out of and in opposition to plantation violence. This program is offered in conjunction with Alfonso Ossorio: Line and Lineage (October 23, 2026–April 11, 2027) in Gallery 1120 at the Harvard Art Museums and Knowledge Is Myth: Chimeric Continuities (October 1–December 13, 2026) at the Carpenter Center for Visual Arts. This event is part of In Conversation, a series of evening programs that feature local and international curators, artists, scholars, and more. Running from September through April, these events highlight our temporary exhibitions, permanent collections, and a range of creative voices.

title: Beginner NY Salsa
description: Classes will be broken into 5 sections at Level 1. New sessions start the first Monday of every odd month. Warmup Footwork Review Foundational move for Level 1 On2 Linear Salsa (of which there are 7) Dance with Music Philosophically things to be on the lookout for, the importance of melding footwork and partner-work when dancing Salsa, the importance of spaced repetition, the importance of tying everything to Social dancing, and personal convolutional schemes to try to attenuate the lead/follow dichotomy. No partner required. *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. *Students who purchase a membership for the Dance Complex will get that $25 taken off their 10 class new student rate, bringing it down to $85. Cost: $23 Single Class | $85 for 5-Class Package | $130 for 10-Class Package | $110 for new student 10-class package Cash, Venmo (@Brendan-Folan), Zelle (bjfoley21@gmail.com) REGISTRATION: Not Required, Drop-Ins Welcome What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Linear Salsa is a hybrid dance that comes from Mambo (a Cuban style that was popularized in the 1950’s NYC Palladium). NY Mambo is a marriage of footwork and partner-work from Cuba (Aftro-Cuban movements, Cuban Son) and the U.S. (Jazz, Swing). Salsa is a marketing term popularized in the 1970’s to commodify all Latin music and dance to a U.S. audience. Circular Salsa primarily comes from the Cuban dance Casino, which itself originates from Cuban Son. Salsa is by nature transformational, multinational, and multigenerational, embodying the shared heritage of Latin music. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I was the assistant teacher of this class for over 2 years under Ricardo Contreras. I’ve been taking classes from Juan Lopez for over 7 years. I started my Salsa journey learning New York Style Salsa On2 in Worcester. I also work at the Havana Club

title: Live Blues & Roots Music Returns to Harvard Square: Wednesday Nights @ The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar
description: The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar and The Barrett Anderson Band are excited to announce a new weekly series, Blues & Roots Wednesdays , bringing live music back home to historic Harvard Square. “Cambridge, our fair city, and I share deep roots, and I’m thrilled to find a new musical home at The Sea Hag,” says Massachusetts-based singer/guitarist, Barrett Anderson. “Good music and good food are two of our most basic, fundamental needs,” he continues, “What great joy they give us. I am so happy to revel in that every Wednesday night with my dearest musical friends, and Kari and her incredible team at The Sea Hag. We go way back together, and I can’t imagine all the fun we have ahead.” Indeed, Anderson has strong connections to this scene. He remembers: “My first professional experience came when I was 15, backing up Muddy Waters’ band alums Pinetop Perkins and Bob Margolin at the original House of Blues on Winthrop Street. A few months after that I began busking, you’d often find me in Brattle Square or by the pit. This would have been mid/late 90s.” While still a teen, Anderson was a member of The Monster Mike Welch Band and Ronnie Earl & The Broadcasters (“Ronnie was my guitar hero. Then he was my teacher, then my boss. Now he’s my musical Father,” Anderson says), before eventually starting The Barrett Anderson Band in 2007. Anderson won a Boston Music Award (2013 Blues Artist of the Year), was on the Billboard charts (2020’s live album Hynoboogie spent 3 weeks on the Billboard Blues Album chart, peaking at #6), and was nominated for a Blues Music Award (2023 Band of the Year with Anthony Geraci & The Boston Blues All-Stars), all the while playing nationally, internationally, and locally in Cambridge and the greater Boston area. In addition to the musical roots, long-time locals may recognize Anderson from a decade serving tables and bartending at The Sea Hag’s sister establishment, Grendel’s Den, or from Abodeon, the mid-century modern shop started by his family. description: Captioned performance. Based on the true story of Katherine Ann Power and Clare Schroeder, this gripping new drama follows two women bound by a single, life-altering moment. It’s 1970. Majestic Healing Pathways™ is the foundational care model that guides all of Majestic Community Wellness’s programs. It reflects our belief that healing is a right — not a privilege — and that healing happens most sustainably when care is consistent, culturally grounded, and rooted in community. Developed in response to gaps in traditional health and wellness systems, Majestic Healing Pathways™ centers the lived experiences of Black and Brown communities who face disproportionate stress, trauma, and barriers to care. The model honors the reality that healing is not a single intervention, but a pathway built over time through breath, movement, rest, relationship, and choice. title: Somatic Movement with Mariah Sabir
description: Somatic Movement is a welcoming space to slow down, reconnect with your body, and explore movement from the inside out. Through grounding, breath, gentle movement, rest, and moments of stillness, you’ll be invited to notice what your body needs and move in ways that feel supportive to you. Rather than focusing on how movement looks, this practice centers how it feels—creating space to release tension, support nervous system regulation, and build greater connection with yourself. Each class explores themes such as boundaries, self-trust, rest, joy, transition, and community. There is no right way to move and nothing to achieve. title: Persia to Iran: History, Politics and Visual Culture of a Civilization in the Headlines
description: How much do our students know about Persia/Iran? This program begins in the ancient period with Achaemenid Persia (550–330 B.C.E.), examining Persian ingenuity, political culture and history as we understand it through the historical and archaeological record. The second part of the program jumps forward in time to 20th- and 21st-century Iran, using the Harvard Peabody Museum’s “From Iran: A Visual Testimony” photographic exhibition as an entry point to more recent historical events and Iranian perspectives on them. We will then delve into Iran’s political history and international relations from the early 20th century forward, noting historical continuities with the past as well as ruptures. Bring your questions and curiosity, regardless of the grade level you teach — this will be a remarkable opportunity to engage with expert historians and curators! This program is in collaboration with the Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology at Harvard.

title: e-flux Architecture—Nick Axel and Nikolaus Hirsch
description: e-flux Architecture—Nick Axel and Nikolaus Hirsch Part of the MIT Fall 2026 Architecture Lecture Series Presented with the Architecture and Urbanism Group Nikolaus Hirsch Nikolaus Hirsch is co-founder and co-editor of e-flux Architecture, as well as the director of the museum Kanal Architecture (formerly CIVA) in Brussels. He was the Dean of Städelschule and Director of the Portikus in Frankfurt and taught at the Architectural Association in London. His architectural work includes the award-winning Dresden Synagogue, Hinzert Document Center, Bockenheimer Depot Theater (with William Forsythe), Cybermohalla Hub in New-Delhi, “Do We Dream Under The Same Sky“ (with Rirkrit Tiravanija at Art Basel / LUMA Arles) and “Becoming Monument” in Fukushima. Hirsch has curated numerous exhibitions such “Wohnungsfrage / Housing Question” at the HKW in Berlin and the German Pavilion at the Architecture Biennale in Venice (“2038”). He is the editor of the Critical Spatial Practice series at Sternberg Press. Nick Axel Nick Axel is an architect, editor, educator, and curator. As Deputy Editor of e-flux Architecture, he has led the development of the platform since its founding in 2016 and undertaken more than 60 editorial projects and publications in collaboration with biennials, museums, universities, and other cultural and research institutions around the world. Nick is also Head of the Architectural Design department at the Gerrit Rietveld Academie in Amsterdam, a three-year educational program at the intersection of architecture, research, theory, and art. He was recently Editor of the 19th International Architecture Exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia, curated by Carlo Ratti, and from 2020–2022, was Curator of Architecture and Chair of the Architectural Advisory Board at the Babyn Yar Holocaust Memorial Center, Kyiv. One of the world’s most popular music genres, “house” is an electronic dance music genre that emerged in Chicago in the late 70s/early 80s following the disco era. The term “house” was derived from The Warehouse, a Chicago club where the music was often played. Though the essence of the dance is purely freestyle, popular steps performed in NYC dance clubs were eventually recognized as “house dance foundation.” Members of NYC’s Dance Fusion were the first to teach house dance, which contributed greatly to house becoming a worldwide phenomenon. description: In this class, you’ll explore earthy Egyptian, Turkish, and American style movements, dynamic combinations, and expressive choreography blending tradition and innovation. The more authentic name for this dance form is raqs sharqi (“dance of the East”), and its roots lie in the Middle and Near East, primarily in Egypt and Turkey. This dance form was introduced to the United States and Europe at the turn of the 20th century, but it was not widely performed or taught until the 1950s and 1960s, when the belly dance craze swept across the U.S. The American cabaret style of belly dance is rooted in the legacy passed down by notable American teachers and performers, who blended Middle Eastern influences with their own innovations and movement styles drawn from diverse dance backgrounds.
